rows.question: How does /proc/sys/kernel/tainted encode taint, and what does this host's 12288 decode to?
rows.statement: /proc/sys/kernel/tainted prints the kernel's taint mask as a decimal number; 0 means untainted and every set bit names one reason. 12288 is 4096 + 8192: bit 12 (letter O, an externally-built or out-of-tree module was loaded) and bit 13 (letter E, an unsigned module was loaded in a kernel that supports module signatures). No other bit is set, so this boot has recorded none of the other events the mask tracks, for example a kernel warning (W, bit 9), an oops (D, bit 7) or a soft lockup (L, bit 14). The kernel's label for E is 'unsigned module'; on this host the modules carry a signature the kernel does not trust (KT3), so the label means 'not verified', not 'no signature'.
rows.action: Read `cat /proc/sys/kernel/tainted` (no privilege) and decode it bit by bit with the tainted-kernels table or `tools/debugging/kernel-chktaint`. Expect 12288 on this host while the nvidia DKMS modules are loaded; any additional bit is a new event to look up, and W, D or L means a warning, oops or lockup to find in `journalctl -k -b 0`.

quotes.text: If that returns ``0``, the kernel is not tainted; any other number indicates the reasons why it is.

rows.question: What does the out-of-tree flag O mean, and when does the kernel set it?
rows.statement: At module load the kernel sets O when the module's modinfo lacks the `intree` tag, that is, when the module was built outside the kernel tree. It prints `<module>: loading out-of-tree module taints kernel.` only for the first such module, and records bit 12 both in the kernel-wide mask and in that module's own taint bits. Modules built by DKMS from a separate source tree carry no `intree` tag [inf: DKMS builds outside the kernel tree; not checked by a source row this round].
rows.host_reading: Boot 0 printed the message for nvidia at 17.5 s; the four nvidia modules load from /lib/modules/7.2.11-arch1-1/updates/dkms/.
rows.action: Expected while nvidia-open-dkms is in use; no repair. Treat an O letter on any module other than the nvidia DKMS set as a finding and name the module from `/sys/module/*/taint`.

quotes.text: pr_warn("%s: loading out-of-tree module taints kernel.\n",
12) ``O`` if an externally-built ("out-of-tree") module has been loaded.

rows.question: What does the unsigned-module flag E mean, when is it set, and why can a module whose modinfo names a signer still set it?
rows.statement: E means a module was loaded whose signature the kernel did not accept, in a kernel built with module signing. The kernel verifies a signature only against keys in its built-in and secondary trusted keyrings. An unsigned module, a module signed with unsupported crypto, or a module signed by a key the kernel does not have is rejected when signatures are enforced; when they are not (permissive mode) it loads, sets E and prints `module verification failed: signature and/or required key missing - tainting kernel`. A signature that fails for other reasons, including a signature mismatch with a known key, stops the load even in permissive mode. So `modinfo -F signer` naming `DKMS module signing key` shows that a signature is attached, not that the kernel trusts the key.
rows.host_reading: sig_enforce N and CONFIG_MODULE_SIG_FORCE not set (permissive); nvidia printed the verification-failed line at 17.5 s; all four nvidia modules carry E and a DKMS signer. Which keyring check failed is not captured: the trusted keyrings were not read this round.
rows.action: Read-only: report that the kernel has not verified the nvidia modules' signatures and that E is expected for every boot as the host is configured. Do not suggest key enrolment as a fix without checking how keys reach the secondary keyring on this host: wave-1 CritLearningFrontier reports that with Secure Boot off the kernel does not load MOK keys at all (an unregistered reading of Linux v7.2 security/integrity code, not a source row of this entry), so enrolling the DKMS key may change nothing. Never read the DKMS private key (credential material). Before enabling `module.sig_enforce=1` or a lockdown mode that requires signatures, expect the nvidia modules to be refused at load unless the kernel trusts their key.

quotes.text: modules for which the key is not available and modules that are unsigned are permitted, but the kernel will be marked as being tainted

rows.question: What do the per-module /sys/module/<name>/taint letters mean, and which modules and packages carry them on this host?
rows.statement: Each module keeps its own taint bits, set together with the kernel-wide bit when the module causes a taint, and `/sys/module/<name>/taint` prints them as letters, read-only (mode 0444). The file names which loaded module caused which letter, which the kernel-wide number cannot do.
rows.host_reading: Four modules print OE: nvidia, nvidia_drm, nvidia_modeset, nvidia_uvm, version 615.78.08, files under /lib/modules/7.2.11-arch1-1/updates/dkms/ that no package owns (pacman -Qo exit 1); they are built on the host by dkms 3.4.4-1 from nvidia-open-dkms 615.78.08-1 (pacman -Q).
rows.action: List culprits with `for f in /sys/module/*/taint; do t=$(cat $f); [ -n "$t" ] && echo ${f%/taint} $t; done`. Because pacman owns no file of a DKMS module, check the module version against the installed nvidia-open-dkms and nvidia-utils versions after each kernel or driver update; a mismatch is a finding for the update-safety checklist.

rows.question: Can a taint flag be cleared, and how?
rows.statement: Not while the kernel runs. The kernel stays tainted after the cause is undone, for example after unloading the module. `add_taint` only sets bits, and a write to /proc/sys/kernel/tainted (CAP_SYS_ADMIN only) adds the written bits through `add_taint` rather than replacing the mask; no code in kernel/panic.c clears a bit. The mask starts again from the kernel's built-in initial value only at the next boot [inf: from the static initialiser of tainted_mask], and on this host the nvidia modules set O and E again at every boot that loads them. Unloading a module can also leave a trace in later oops reports [unverified: wave-1 critic finding, not a source row of this entry].
rows.host_reading: O and E were set at 17.5 s of boot 0 and are still set at capture time.
rows.action: Do not unload modules or write the sysctl to 'clear' taint: unloading changes nothing in the mask, and a write can only add flags. Compare readings within one boot; a value that grows within a boot is a new event.

quotes.text: Note the kernel will remain tainted even after you undo what caused the taint

rows.question: What does taint mean for a kernel bug report or an oops reading, and what does the operator do?
rows.statement: The kernel prints its taint letters in the `Tainted:` field of the `CPU:` line of every bug, oops and panic report, and developers often ignore reports from tainted kernels; the documentation asks reporters to reproduce problems with an untainted kernel. On this host an oops will show `O` and `E` because of the nvidia modules. The host itself is not harmed by this (HEALTHY); the limit is on upstream reports from such a boot.
rows.host_reading: Every boot that loads the nvidia DKMS modules is tainted O and E (KT1 to KT5).
rows.action: For a kernel problem meant for upstream, first try to reproduce it with an untainted kernel, that is, a boot in which the nvidia modules are not loaded (an operator decision), and report that boot's log. Read the `Tainted:` field of an oops with the KT1 table; on this host O and E alone are expected and do not by themselves point at the fault.

quotes.text: That's why bug reports from tainted kernels will often be ignored by developers, hence try to reproduce problems with an untainted kernel.
